study: INTENDED: Cesarini, Lindqvist, Notowidigdo & Ostling, 'Wealth, Health, and Child Development: Evidence from Administrative Data on Swedish Lottery Players' (QJE 2016). ACTUAL FILE CONTENT: Pinkovskiy & Sala-i-Martin, 'Lights, Camera,... Income! Estimating Poverty Using National Accounts, Survey Means, and Lights' (NBER WP 19831, Jan 2014).

period: 2000-2013 (TFR/ASFR/parity 2001-2013; education-specific 2007-2011); 31 European countries plus the United States (32 total)
fertility_outcome: log TFR, log age-specific fertility rates (ASFR, 15-19 ... 40-44), log parity-specific fertility rates (first/second/third birth), log education-specific fertility rates (ISCED 0-2/3-4/5-6); log-log fixed-effects models yielding elasticities
units: percent change in TFR per 1% increase in lagged total unemployment rate (elasticity, %); equivalently ~-0.011 births/woman per 1 pp unemployment; cumulative ~-0.047 births (~3% TFR decline) over the +4.29 pp rise in unemployment 2007-2013
sample_n: 32 countries (31 European + US); panel of country-years 2000-2013 (max 13 years/country, some country-years missing; TFR/ASFR/parity for 32 countries 2001-2013; EPU for 8 countries; CCI for 24 countries; bond yields for 30 countries, Southern-Europe models; education-specific for 19 countries 2007-2011). No individual-level N; macro panel.
rob_overall: Credible descriptive macro evidence of a procyclical, negative fertility-unemployment/uncertainty association; NOT fit for identifying the C.1.a pure income-as-normal-good effect. Useful only as CONTEXT and as a negative signpost that routes to C.5.a (economic uncertainty/unemployment).

study: Dettling & Kearney, "House Prices and Birth Rates", J. Public Economics (2014)
shock: MSA-level house-price change (lagged, year of conception), instrumented with Saiz (2012) housing-supply elasticity interacted with the national house-price trend
fertility_outcome: ln(MSA-group-year fertility rate): births per 1000 women age 20-44, dated to year of conception; also split by first/second/higher parity and by race/ethnicity
units: percent change in current-period fertility rate per $10,000 MSA house-price increase, among homeowners (100% home-ownership cells); OLS baseline. IV counterpart is +7.2% (beta1=0.0723). Net effect at mean 44% ownership = +0.8%
sample_n: 9,240 MSA-group-year cells (10 years x 6 race/age groups x 154 MSAs) for the 1997-2006 baseline; births from Vital Statistics Natality Files (near-universe of U.S. live births)

study: Kearney & Wilson, "Male Earnings, Marriageable Men, and Nonmarital Fertility: Evidence from the Fracking Boom", REStat 2018 (NBER WP 23408)
period: Births conceived 1997-2012 (PUMA x year panel; fracking boom concentrated post-2005)
design: Reduced-form panel OLS at PUMA x year level (2,044 PUMAs x 16 years), with PUMA fixed effects, state-by-year effects, and time-varying PUMA controls (sex ratio, log house price, race and education shares). Identification off simulated new fracking production (geology-driven shale-play exposure x year), measured in $1,000 per capita. Also reports an auxiliary IV (production as instrument for per-capita earnings) for comparison to Black et al. 2013.
fertility_outcome: overall/marital/nonmarital birth rates (births per 1,000 women 18-34) plus non-marital birth share
units: additional total births per 1,000 women age 18-34 per $1,000 simulated new production per capita
sample_n: Balanced panel of 2,044 PUMAs over 1997-2012 (~32,700 PUMA-year birth obs); earnings first-stage uses 29,471 PUMA/year cells from 45 states; 611 of 2,057 PUMAs had positive new production (ND and MT and Webb County TX excluded)
rob_overall: Moderate -- credible causal estimate of the effect of a local positive economic shock on fertility, but weak for isolating a pure non-labor income effect from the wage/earnings channel.
